title: First hearing the band, Good Time Jazz, her novel and George's contract
summary: Tait recalls the overwhelming first night at the Beverly Cavern, struggles to name a record executive, discusses the character modelled on George in her novel, and the exclusive contract she arranged. The tape then shifts to Bob Green.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: No, not Amherst. Not Williams. Amherst isn't in Vermont, it's in my own state. Um, not Bennington, that's a women's college. I can't remember them all, but there were a great many. There were a great many of them. Then there was a St. Paul's, a preparatory school, prep school in Massachusetts very late. Uh, uh, uh, uh. Like that? Yes, Alvin Kershaw arranged the date. Oh, that's funny, he's never on that. And, uh, no, he's moved somewhere else. I don't know where. I'll have to ask George. Isn't he in Peterborough? Not anymore. He was. Oh yes, and of course the band played in Peterborough. They played at a very informal type thing in Peterborough for, uh, for Al Kershaw. Uh, and in the middle of winter, ooh. Describe for me if you can. The very first time you had, when you said you went down to Los Angeles, had them in bed. I can't. I can't. I can't. It was such an overwhelming thing. It really was. It's not a thing I can put in words. Uh, I went in, I got there, they told me, when I cried, I called them on the phone and I said, must I make reservations? They said, yes, but don't expect us to hold them past a half hour before we open. Get here early? Well, I got there way early. And, uh, I remember I asked one of the cocktail waitresses if it would be possible for me to meet George Lewis. And she said, oh, of course. And she called him, uh, over and, uh, we sat at the bar and had a drink. And, of course, I was, I couldn't believe it was true. And, uh, Lawrence was there, and drag, and the whole group. And, um, George showed me just where to sit so I'd get the best sound and so forth. And he, I mentioned a number of numbers, he played them all for me. And, uh, it, it was overwhelming. It really was. I think, I think it's almost impossible for anyone to describe how they felt the first time they heard that real George Lewis group, with Lawrence and the whole group. It's, it's something you can't put in words. I went back to the hotel, as I say, and the world was all golden sound, you know? Oh. And, uh, I could hear it in my ears all night. Yeah. And, uh, it, it, it, to me, it was a, it's a very overwhelming experience, if you dig that music and really love it. Yes, I know. Let me think, there was one thing, this is something you may or may not know about this, and I just can't remember the man's name. Um, uh, what's his name, that record company? Good Time Jazz. Oh! Now, you remember, there's a very nice man, he's sort of fat. Yeah, uh, sure, Dave Stewart. Not Dave Stewart. Not Dave Stewart. Oh. No, no. Um, what is his name? Keith again. Yeah. A very nice man, kind of. Yeah, he's fat, uh, distinctly fat. But he, uh, not, not Mr. Koenig, there's another man, there's another man in that. Oh, Mr. Koenig. But he, he, he was, he was down here a year ago, and then, he told me that, that Good Time Jazz had recorded the George Lewis band playing in the Beverly Cabins for a year. Beverly Cabins for a regular concert, around about that time, 54. And that they were going to- No, I think it was before that. Maybe. It was before that. They recorded him there, and I believe they, uh, But the records never sold like a day, anyway. Whether they recorded him in, uh, at the Hangover Club in, uh, San Francisco or not, I don't know. I know Lester came up there and George refused to sign a contract with him. Uh, an exclusive contract. And, uh, but, very fat. I just can't- Isn't that funny? I always have trouble remembering that man. I can't think who you mean. He came- You know, there is a picture in my mind of a short, very fat man, but he doesn't tie up with anything in particular. He now sort of has his own record company, some kind of thing. And, uh, he was responsible for the issue of some of the early George Rose records, where he did Willie the Weeper and, uh, the- Yes, that was a good time, yes. But I just- Doesn't matter anyway. It's not important. No. It's- It's- It's- It's- Um. Um. Um. Um. Well, one thing I did want to ask you about was about the character of David in the Five Moved Stones. Well, the character of David is no one in—that is not based on any individual. But the character of Grant is more or less based on George Lewis. The character of who? Grant. The grandfather. Oh, I see. The grandfather. Yes. Not, of course, completely. I mean, George is a well-known clarinetist, and Grant in Five Moved Stones was just a man who played banjo locally, and there were some differences. But as far as his character and his personality, I admit it was frankly pretty much George Lewis. So much so that Molly Moon came down here not long ago. Her husband is the national director of publicity for the NAACP. And she went to Preservation Hall in the hope of hearing George. She didn't know him and hadn't heard him. And she walked in the hall and she said, there's Gramp! And—but that character is. But the character of David, who is the protagonist in the book, is not anyone in particular. The young man, sort of a composite of, you know—let me just ask you one other thing I had in mind. George did have an exclusive contract at one time, but— That's right. Do you know anything about that? I—I—oh, yes, I set it up. I had been wanting George to settle down to one company for a long time. And I went and I talked with Norman Grant. Ooh! But we finally set up a fairly, uh, a fairly nice arrangement. It was for two years. And it called for two or three records a year. I've—I've forgotten. I mean albums. And, uh, at the time of its expiration, Norman, uh, had, uh, was sold to that other company. And then George's health was very bad at that time. Which is when he was having those bad angina attacks. It didn't seem safe to—or fair, really, to the company. Although, heaven knows when the day that record companies, um, with one exception, which is Alfred Lyon, God love it. Uh, the day that record companies are completely fair to artists is the day that I'm really— Okay, we're just—I'll just say this is, uh, January the 5th, 1969. And I'm interviewing Bob Green. Right.
